review_text_raw:
I've only played one case. Maybe it gets better but I already hate it. This is a game that saw [i]Papers Please[/i] and a Telltale game and thought: these should be one thing. They shouldn't. It wants to have the humanism of a game that is mostly just a postmodern exploration of character ([i]Her Story, Analogue: A Hate Story[/i]), but it also wants you to make binary data choices on which set of data to pass on to your superior without being given enough information to know how it will be interpreted.

[i]Papers Please[/i] presents very clear outcomes for the majority of your choices and the moral weight they have and gives a context for why a choice must be made anyway.  By presenting the status quo of a job which you must do for a family who could starve, the game allows for depth of story, a context for why things must be as they are and real stakes for the choices that are made.

Telltale games often don't pre-empt the outcomes of your choices, but often these choices are superfluous because what matters is the character drama. But the thing is that the games sensationalize these choices and make them feel like they could matter, even when they don't. This character could die instead of this one, you might find out a different set of information, but the structure of the story and the characters' movement through it remains intact. 

When you mash them up what you get is a completely unnuanced yes-no/good-bad moral choice system ala Fable in a world that resembles the real one too closely for that to not be cringe-worthy. Only the binary isn't good/bad because as someone who is already spying on someone and potentially ruining their life just to test if you can get access to the next document by adding chunks that seem only tangentially related but will be interpreted as reason to call the police, you're always bad. And if that's what the game's political critique boils down to, then I got it. Thumbs up.

"Are they really terrorists?" the game's description asks. And the answer is no. I could have guessed that from the bugged out clip following her getting on a bus that only played the second time I started a new game because the first one I hit a dead end and had no choice but to just start adding data at random hoping something would trigger only to have to google and find out it was a known bug and I just had to restart from the start. So thanks, I hate it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This review won't matter much in the long run, but [i]Orwell[/i] just seems way over-rated to me. I'll try to explain why.

The story is needlessly convoluted, but let's set that aside.

The core gameplay mechanic (if you want to call it that) is dragging text from the right side of the screen to the left side of the screen. [b][u]That is all[/u][/b]: click to open windows to find text, then click and drag some portions of text that have been pre-selected and pre-highlighted as potentially relevant. When you drag text to the left side of the screen, it gets uploaded to the Orwell database as one of the results of your investigations. The Steam Trailer involves a bit of role-playing that doesn't quite represent gameplay accurately in this regard.

What really frustrated me was just how clumsy some of the most thematically important mechanics are. Sometimes, you find 2 "datachunks" of text (let's call them A and B) that conflict with each other, and you have to decide which one to upload. Your choice makes a difference to how the story unfolds, and affects people's lives. People can be arrested or die based on what you upload. The choices you make in situations like this constitute 100% of the moral complexity that [i]Orwell[/i] intends to confront you with. These decisions are central to the narrative, and to the player's experience.

Here's what's super lame: sometimes, when you find text A, and [i][u]before you could even possibly have an opportunity to see B[/u][/i]. the game says "A conflicts with [u]an unknown datachunk[/u]." This clumsy mechanic is in tension with the most basic plot-point of the game. The whole plot of the game is that The Nation needs [u]you[/u] to track down information and to decide what information goes into Orwell's databases. But what gameplay tells you is that [i]before you do anything[/i], Orwell already knows all the information that's out there, and knows when a conflict will arise, even when you (as the Investigator who is supposed to be influencing the story) have no idea yourself that B exists, and have done no detective work to suggest to Orwell that B exists. The whole thing is on (branching) rails, and your decisions amount to nothing more than selecting A vs. B, when Orwell can predict the conflict between A and B in advance. This means your detective work is essentially irrelevant; Orwell has done it all in advance, but won't share it with you. All that's left to matter is the choice between A and B.

One solution would've been to just let you resolve conflicts later: suppose that first you find and upload A, then later you find B, and you make a decision about whether to keep A in the database or replace it with B. But that would disrupt the game's ability to proceed with the narrative in a way that approximates a real-time unfolding of events. What the game wants to do is unfold the story as soon as you upload info to Orwell's database, irreversibly. If you upload A (whether or not you've seen B) then the A-chain of events begins. As a result, the game [b]has[/b] to tell you in advance that there's a conflict, so that you can "choose" which on-rails narrative will unfold.

So, my conclusion is that this is a game that is, fundamentally, poorly built. The core gameplay mechanics are kludges, patched together to facilitate the unfolding of the (branching) on-rails narrative. There are some choices to make, but the bulk of "investigative" gameplay is meaningless: this is a slideshow in games' clothing.

The Steam Trailer involves a bit of role-playing that doesn't quite represent gameplay accurately in this regard. What really frustrated me was just how clumsy some of the most thematically important mechanics are. Sometimes, you find 2 "datachunks" of text (let's call them A and B) that conflict with each other, and you have to decide which one to upload. Your choice makes a difference to how the story unfolds, and affects people's lives. People can be arrested or die based on what you upload. The choices you make in situations like this constitute 100% of the moral complexity that [i]Orwell[/i] intends to confront you with. These decisions are central to the narrative, and to the player's experience. Here's what's super lame: sometimes, when you find text A, and [i][u]before you could even possibly have an opportunity to see B[/u][/i]. the game says "A conflicts with [u]an unknown datachunk[/u]." This clumsy mechanic is in tension with the most basic plot-point of the game. The whole plot of the game is that The Nation needs [u]you[/u] to track down information and to decide what information goes into Orwell's databases. But what gameplay tells you is that [i]before you do anything[/i], Orwell already knows all the information that's out there, and knows when a conflict will arise, even when you (as the Investigator who is supposed to be influencing the story) have no idea yourself that B exists, and have done no detective work to suggest to Orwell that B exists. The whole thing is on (branching) rails, and your decisions amount to nothing more than selecting A vs. B, when Orwell can predict the conflict between A and B in advance. This means your detective work is essentially irrelevant; Orwell has done it all in advance, but won't share it with you. All that's left to matter is the choice between A and B. One solution would've been to just let you resolve conflicts later: suppose that first you find and upload A, then later you find B, and you make a decision about whether to keep A in the database or replace it with B. But that would disrupt the game's ability to proceed with the narrative in a way that approximates a real-time unfolding of events. What the game wants to do is unfold the story as soon as you upload info to Orwell's database, irreversibly. If you upload A (whether or not you've seen B) then the A-chain of events begins. As a result, the game [b]has[/b] to tell you in advance that there's a conflict, so that you can "choose" which on-rails narrative will unfold. So, my conclusion is that this is a game that is, fundamentally, poorly built. The core gameplay mechanics are kludges, patched together to facilitate the unfolding of the (branching) on-rails narrative. There are some choices to make, but the bulk of "investigative" gameplay is meaningless: this is a slideshow in games' clothing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell is basically just working but with more steps. Thankfully I got it on sale, but I wouldn’t recommend it as I felt I was just doing admin work the whole time. Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The Good: Amazing world development, excellent sense of tension, powerful story, and genuinely intriguing.  Also, it would have been easy to over-moralize, instead they make their moral point in small ways.  You stop a bombing but accidentally used the fact someone said they'd "torture" a friend jokingly to have them declared a potentially dangerous person.  It comes off as a more intelligent and incisive commentary on the Surveilance State, the NSA, PRISM and the like because it wasn't completely one-sided.  

The Bad:  The intro shows a watch_Dogs style "popup information about people walking by a camera" interface that looks awesome.  This is the only time you will see it.  While the interface as it is has varied info sources using the cameras that keep getting mentioned might be nice!  On the other hand maybe that's a political statement, that you leave enough intel they don't need CCTV everywhere to track you... I don't know.  
It's pretty short, though at this price point I forgive that.

The Ugly:  Episodic construction means you will be waiting on tenterhooks for the next one.

Get this if:  You liked the idea behind Westport Independent, you watch Mr. Robot, If you thought Watch_Dogs and CtOS were a fascinating idea poorly delivered,  If you like cyberpunk in general.

Suggested price point:  Pay full price, you won't regret the ride.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" is an outstanding game that had me hooked from start to finish. The developers have masterfully crafted a gripping and unsettling story that tackles contemporary issues such as surveillance, privacy, and ethics.

The gameplay mechanics are unique and innovative. As a player, you take on the role of an investigator who sifts through data and analyzes information to uncover threats to national security. Throughout the game, you are faced with moral decisions that significantly impact the storyline. These choices are often challenging and thought-provoking, making the game a deeply engaging experience.

The atmosphere of the game is excellently executed. The visual design and soundtrack contribute to creating a dense and suspenseful mood. What is particularly impressive is how realistic and believable the world of "Orwell" feels. You truly feel like a part of this dystopian society.

Another highlight is the storytelling. The narrative is thrilling and full of twists that constantly surprise you. The characters are well-developed, and their fates are compelling. You quickly form an emotional connection with the characters and find yourself rooting for them.

Overall, "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" is a masterpiece that not only entertains but also makes you think. It is a game that stays with you long after you have finished playing. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an intelligent and captivating game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is an investigative game akin to a visual novel. You play as The Investigator, someone whose job it is to use the powerful Orwell surveillance system to solve crimes – or in this case, solve a particular crime. You see, a bomb was set off in Freedom Plaza in The Nation, killing three people, and it is your job to try and catch the bomber before they can kill anyone else.

Orwell is more like an interactive novel than an ordinary video game – the game is wholly centered around reading text for about four and a half hours, and while it has more meaningful interaction than most visual novels, the actual gameplay itself is very simple and not very action-oriented. It is a very cerebral experience, and if reading lots of text isn’t your cup of tea, this is not the game for you.

You start out with a single person of interest – a young woman who left the Plaza shortly before the bomb went off. She was a protester who had been arrested for attacking a police officer, but who wasn’t prosecuted for it due to lack of evidence. It quickly becomes clear that not all is as it seems, and it seems unlikely that she personally was the bomber – but she has past associations with a group known as Thought, an anti-government group which often engages in extremist rhetoric. But are they really the sort of people who would kill people? Or are they just innocent bystanders coincidentally caught up in the investigation?

Orwell is a very ambiguous game, and it is precisely this ambiguity which really makes the game work. Thought is upset about living in a surveillance state, but it is clear from your perspective as The Investigator that the system is designed to be humane in many ways – the investigator passes on information to someone else, whose job it is to analyze the data. You cannot investigate people who aren’t targets – unless someone has been designated as suspicious by actual data, you cannot collect data at all them, nor are you allowed to go snooping through their things. But if they are a target of interest, you have nigh unlimited authority to go snooping. And while the state is clearly a bit authoritarian, it is also clear that the system works – crime has gone down, and you can catch several criminals over the course of the game who really did do bad things. The person on the other end, who helps to determine whether or not the data is really indicative of wrongdoing, is a genuinely nice person who cares about people and who urges you to collect more data. The leader of The Nation appears to genuinely be trying to help out neighboring states.

But all of this is muddied with the ambiguity of the fact that not everyone in the government is nice, and the general sinister nature of your surveillance. Your actions do have consequences, and it is clear that if you made the wrong decisions, you could potentially feed people bad data and get people put in jail – and the choice of whether or not to feed people bad data, and the impression you leave the government on people, is dependent on what data you give them.

The game, thus, is a combination of an investigation and a moral choice system – you are not only investigating who might be the bomber, but also deciding what is and is not relevant, what should and should not be part of the investigation, and you have the power to wrongfully put people in jail or put people in danger. The very simple gameplay of choosing what pieces of highlighted information to put into a database from various documents, webpages, emails, and phone and text conversations thus takes on a great deal of weight, and makes you think about what you’re doing in a very different way from other investigatory games, as you think of it not only in terms of true/false, but also whether the information morally belongs in the hands of the government.

The game’s gameplay also shows how a system like that can lead to paranoia, as you see people engage in a lot of extremist rhetoric and it is easy to jump to conclusions and morally convict someone in your mind who didn’t do anything worse than complain, as well as how easy it is to prejudge someone in the opposite direction as well, making you think more positively of them than they truly deserve. And it puts stress on the player as well – you cannot take back your actions, so if you incorrectly present someone as a dangerous criminal, you can’t fix it and have to live with the consequences.

How humane the system is – and who is in the right and wrong – is a complicated question that the game ultimately doesn’t answer for itself, but which the player answers via their actions throughout the game. Like “The Lady or the Tiger”, the way the player responds to the story really reflects as much on the player’s own evaluation of humanity, and how they weigh the risks and benefits of a system like that. Rather than being preachy about how evil the system is, the game also shows why people might like a system like that and want it to be implemented. It is perhaps the most even-handed presentation of the subject matter I’ve seen, and it achieves this by putting the player in the seat of someone who might be a part of such a system and showing just how ambiguous the system can be and how much power they wield, both how dangerous it can be if misused but how beneficial it can be if used appropriately.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Whoa! What a morally complex game! I've spent so much time thinking about some decisions. Some i did not think through, some turned out pretty well! It was great piecing all the information together and even if i missed some stuff, i'd say i've done a pretty decent job.

Spoiler warnings ahead.

What is right in this game? I honestly have no idea. The Orwell system did spy a lot on it's citizens (if only them lol), however if graphs are to be believed, the safety did increase and quite a lot. I even prevented one bombing and saved some lives!

Even if that bombing was in the end meant to fight the corrupted attempts at surveillance - it was only partially justified. Did the ends justify the means? It's easy to say these few sacrifices of people through bombings might have been justified.

However, as an investigator, it molded my first perception of The Thought group in a negative view. But then, without the hacker and other people's involvement would i (or for that matter anyone) be able to expose the unethical use of surveillance?

Who knows. But then, it seemed like Abraham wasn't this ''great hero'' either. He was paranoic of living in that Germany town, because everyone knew someone? I did not get his motivations there.
He even left his loving family - his wife and daughter who were quite deeply affected by that, so he can preach on university about thoughts being free? He also got traumatised in that Rhosen tech company, after he saw the failures of the earlier Orwell version, yet he became involved and sped up the process.

If he was so ''understanding'' of ethics and thoughts being free, i'm sure he would've noticed that the other employers did not care about them.
Then he gave upgrade to Orwell and was surprised that they did workarounds for his ethical codexes. It seems like his own thoughts weren't free in the first place and his decisions were quite irrational, motivated by fear.

Honestly, he and Thought members, Delacroix and likely other higher ups, many other people and finally me as investigator were partially to blame. I feel like a decent amount of people were truly in fault.

ALSO, i think if i didn't stop that bomb, the diplomatic talks abroad would have not worked. I mean sure, they were in part planned to keep Orwell on working, but it also seems like the Nation was doing some charitable actions in other countries too.

At first i was supportive of Orwell system, howere the issue was with the higher ups being unethical jerks - with the advisor guy Symes being actually really nice guy and with nice family. I was glad he made it out safe out of his house and i hope he could live his life somewhat normally afterwards.

If the Delacroix and perhaps others would have been more decent human beings and actually did have a solid ethical codex, that is well reviewed scientifically, then i believe Orwell could had been actually a successful surveillance system with way better results.

In the first half of the game i was really surprised of how well the system worked. I did stop the third bombing after all. It definitely could get some improvements, like possibility of retracing data (due to new informations) and retracing arrests (i felt bad for some of them and, based on achievements, i might've arrested one or more people unjustly).

This game gave me interesting insight into surveillance. With more twixes and solid, peer reviewed codex - that one has to strictly abide to, i believe this could work much better. It already did, based on the decreasing crime rates - i'm 100% sure it had caught many criminals off guard, since i was able to infiltrate the devices of the head of security herself.

MAN! What a game! I certainly did not expect much from it, but it had blown my expectations! Honestly i think it's going to land in my favourites. Excellent game.

I believe the game posed some really morally gray views. It's hard for me to say that one person / side is right and others wrong. I did not expect such complexity and it kind of reminds me of Attack on Titan moral dilemmas. It feels like each approach has it's downsides, but also justifications and i love that. In the end there might be no one single right choice to make. Instead it may be up to our egos and making the choice we would regret the least.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I do not recommend this game. Here's why.
First of all - it's boring. It really is. Gameplay-wise it offers just web browsing, reading stuff and clicking. Telltale's games do not offer much in gameplay, but at least you can watch pretty nice visuals and be engaged in the story. Here you just click and browse. Click and browse. And then browse and click a bit more. When I want to read (and I love reading) I read books, not games.
Second thing - visuals. Yes, the game's style and interface are aesthetically pleasing. But... first developers show lack of any effort to make the game rich in gameplay, then do the same with graphics. Yes they use nice colors. Yes the font is elegant. But it's easy to see how it was designed to be made quickly and effortlessly with those simple vectors. Perfect square on plain background is also aesthetically pleasant, but it doesn't show any craftsmanship. And yes, the art style is not crucial for game to be good. But it helps. Especially when game lacks in other areas.
And finally - the story itself. Game puts in you in the shoes of government worker. And it feels like work to play this game. And what kind of work is that? Spying on people and playing a god. Nothing to be proud of. Looks like you're the part of totalitarian machine, aimed at controlling the people. Taken straight from the Orwell's "Year 1984". Which is not necessarily a bad idea, but... the people you spy on are as obnoxious as your job and character you play. So which side developers really take? It looked like whether the game will try to convey I am doing something good, or those terrorist I'm trying to catch are "good" - I will be very, very disappointed. The "progressive vibe" I started to feel was getting on my nerves, as game was not allowing me to take choices I wanted to take. That I felt would be moral. So it's a frustrating experience, before it finally gets so boring you just stop playing.

Perfect square on plain background is also aesthetically pleasant, but it doesn't show any craftsmanship. And yes, the art style is not crucial for game to be good. But it helps. Especially when game lacks in other areas. And finally - the story itself. Game puts in you in the shoes of government worker. And it feels like work to play this game. And what kind of work is that? Spying on people and playing a god. Nothing to be proud of. Looks like you're the part of totalitarian machine, aimed at controlling the people. Taken straight from the Orwell's "Year 1984". Which is not necessarily a bad idea, but... the people you spy on are as obnoxious as your job and character you play. So which side developers really take? It looked like whether the game will try to convey I am doing something good, or those terrorist I'm trying to catch are "good" - I will be very, very disappointed. The "progressive vibe" I started to feel was getting on my nerves, as game was not allowing me to take choices I wanted to take. That I felt would be moral. So it's a frustrating experience, before it finally gets so boring you just stop playing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]English:[/b]
The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

その犯人がOrwellを非難したところで犠牲者を生んだテロリストの言説として空虚に響くだけでしょう。
また[spoiler]後半での展開も炎上からの破壊行動が容易く起きるのなら[/spoiler]“監視”の程度も大した事はないのでは？と感じます。監視なんぞ知るかという人が[spoiler]暴徒化したのだとしたら[/spoiler]、そもそも犯罪率の低下とは何だったんでしょうか。

台詞送りやスキップが無いのはリアルタイムの盗聴という表現であるにしても快適性を損ないますし、こういった部分も作品の魅力を自ら削いでいる様な感じがしてなりません。

review_text_raw:
I love the game mechanics!

However, I wish the game gave players more power to decide what actions to take.

Since you’re just an information collector, the only way to influence the outcome is by choosing not to feed certain information to your supervisor. That limits a lot of freedom because you can't really control what a scripted supervisor thinks. And sometimes, if you don’t feed the plot-required information, the game just stops and waits for you, forcing you to still somewhat follow the intended plot. The illusion of "choice matter" in this case is worse than reading a visual novel.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a classic example of doing wonders using very little. 

It won't blow you away with the graphics, but combined with the immersive, gentle soundtrack that dynamically changes as you play, and a captivating story and well written content, you'll be hooked. 

I've always very much been a fan of slower paced games that involve alot of surrounding story and Orwell provides it in droves, without being a very clumsy political statement by itself. You're dropped into the "Orwell" system and told to go to work investigating a terrorist attack, but there are no clear cut moral choices, you read the information given to you, submit what is pertinent and do your job, all the while slowly being drawn into your role as an investigator - all without a single action sequence or quicktime event. 

If atmospheric games are your thing, give it a go. The interface is clean, intuitive, the soundtrack is hauntingly beautiful, and the whole story will keep you glued to your government workstation for the duration.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

Good start, bad pacing; this game has mostly positive reviews because it is well made and a great concept, but if you're looking for an evolution on Papers, Please then move along; the game is way too story heavy to be any fun and the development of the story is predictable and boring.  Entire chucks on the game where you do nothing but read exposition on a situation you have no emotional investment in.  This is my biggest contention with the game as intends to challenge the player's morality, but doesn't do so in a meaningful way (for me, at least).

Well made but it just won't scratch that bureaucratic, 'cog-in-the-machine' itch that you might be looking for, and in that regard I'm not too sure who this game is for.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

review_text_raw:
This game had a very interesting and intense storyline, and was a lot of fun to play.  It didn't take too long (I finished it in roughly three, one-hour increments) and if I'd had the time to sit for all three hours, I'd have finished it in a  single sitting.  The graphics are good, and the mix of platform-style investigation tools is a lot of fun.  

The sequence of events is locked in, so you're pretty much at the mercy of finding what you're supposed to find.  While it is listed as "choices matter", that should not lead to the inference that the choices are variable...basically, either you extract the right information and complete the game, or you suck and the bad guys win.  

At any rate, $10 is a super reasonable price for this game.  If there were another "case" or scenario, or even a variation on the kind of investigation, I'd pay another $10 right now.  If you're looking to kill an afternoon, this game is a good choice.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Guys!  Perhaps this may come as a shock to some of you but, in case you didn’t know, this game has a bit of an agenda….[/b] 
Ok ok, joking aside I bought Orwell a while back when it fell below my “if I buy this and don’t like it, I won’t feel any great loss” threshold.  It sat in my library untouched until a rainy day when I didn’t feel like getting into anything too involved.  I say this to admit that I went into this with pretty bland expectations.  

I generally view games like this the way I do a book from an unknown author, but that has a premise I like.  I knew going in that the game makers had a point to make and even though it was a point I generally agree with, I was a little wary.  [i]I don’t like being preached at, so I wasn’t sure if I was going to spend the entire game being beat over the head with the rhetoric bat whilst being presented with billboards saying in big bold letters “Hey look, the authors feel very strongly about this” at every turn or if the game would have any merit beyond the political statement.[/i]  [b]I’m very thankful to say that this game was far more than just a tray upon which to serve political and social commentary and it was even very clever in doing so.[/b]

So why did I start out with all that waffle about political commentary?  Because I want to set the tone for how I approached the game and the preconceptions I had going in.  I went into the experience thinking that I pretty much had them figured out and that I would easily be able to see through any “hard choices with lasting consequences” to what the authors were really trying to sell to the player.  And chapter 1 pretty much was just that.  I “knew” they were trying to get me to suspect a particular person and that they wanted me to assume the simple answer so they could jump out from behind the posterized, low-polygon trees and say “Ha!  See how even with all the information at your fingertips you jumped to the wrong conclusion.”  So naturally I did just the opposite.  Purposefully ignoring what I assumed were red-herrings and by the end of chapter 1, I’d almost lost interest figuring that I had it all figured out.  I was delighted, and a bit disappointed, that I was wrong.  

Starting chapter 2, I was actually engaged in the narrative and was now determined not to be caught off-guard again.  I still knew there was a point to it all, but I wasn’t as sure I knew what that point was.  By the end of the game, I knew what was going on, but because I’d fed information to orwell earlier on that seemed harmless at the time, I’d built a profile on some of the characters that was not incorrect but was misrepresentative.  This led to events playing out in a way that I didn’t want and with no way to go back and correct.  I felt duped, but in a good way.  The game had indeed gotten it’s point across, but in a very subtle and engaging way that left me still feeling that I enjoyed the experience.

So let’s sum this up, shall we? 
•	Orwell was well worth the money
•	Gameplay was not nearly as on-rails as I had expected
•	Story was actually very engaging and believable
•	Plot twists did not feel super-contrived simply to force the player to be wrong for the sake of proving a point.  All the plot twists could have been seen coming I think if the user had paid attention to the details and not just focused on what Orwell highlights.
•	The game actually made me think and didn’t preach it’s point smugly from contrived moral high-ground and I appreciated that.  

Here is where I would usually list a few things that could have been improved, but the game is pretty simple and the UI layout is simple and easy to use.  Some of the “websites” that you visit have clickable links that aren’t obvious… that was kind of annoying, but not too bad.  I’d like to say that I wish you could go back and edit information when you found out it was wrong, but I think it’s integral to the game the concept that YOU are the filter.  If it’s not relevant, accurate, or then you don’t upload it.  If I had one complaint it would be that I sometimes didn’t know what would “trigger” the next event and so sometimes I’d upload something I didn’t really want to just because I thought I had to in order to progress the game.   

All in all, the game took me about 6 hours to play through… you could go longer or shorter, but in the end, it’s not a great investment timewise…. In fact, it practically gives you a good stopping point between chapters.  I highly recommend the game.  It’s worth $7-10 for your time and as a good conversation starter.  Gift it to a friend so you can have a good conversation on the topic.  

Anyway, That’s my 2 cents worth.

-John

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] A very enjoyable game with hidden depth, despite the very simple game mechanics. [/h1]

You investigate persons of interest in a bombing (i.e read a whole bunch and invade peoples' privacy) through their online information and electronic devices via Orwell, The Nations new secret surveilence system. The people and ways you can investigate are not all immediately available, you unlock more options and imformation based on the data you upload and where you are in the story. The gameplay ultimately boils down to drag-and-droping the datachunks (that the game hightlights) that you think are relevent, into Orwell.

While on the surface the game may seem not very challenging or lacking in replayability as some claim, there are subtleties that make Orwell really great.

Such as the fact that you, as the investigator, are the only person who will see the [b] context [/b] of the data you're uploading. Mild episode 1 spoiler: [spoiler] See a woman joking with her boyfriend that she stole his credit card (which she uses to buy a bottle of wine), which he seems mildly annoyed by but seemingly fine with? Upload that into Orwell and all your superiors know is that she "stole a credit card". [/spoiler] Whether or not you think reporting that is morally right or not, it does have an effect on how things turn out for her.
There are several times such as this when the information you can upload is damning, incomplete or inaccurate simply because the datachunk lacks context. There are times when you can use this to your advantage, if say you want to frame someone winkwink.

There are also times where you will encounter "conflicting data chunks", where you have the choice of which one (sometimes if any) you wish to upload. These choices often lead to a person or circumstance being viewed in an entirely different manner. Sometimes it is the drastic difference between someone being seen as a terrorist or an innocent.
This is why it's very important to look very carefully at what a datachunk is really uploading to Orwell and remember you needn't and perhaps shouldn't upload everything.

Overall this game puts you into a position where you have to make a lot of moral decisions around privacy, relevancy, and generally be the judge of everyone you investigate. Your choices/ethics directly and indirectly influence the fate of all the characters you meet.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Original and interesting premise - you are a foreigner sifting through online data and decide which you submit to the investigators. The investigative team is obliged to act on your input, draw conclusions, proceed with investigation, gather more evidence, make arrests...

It all starts as a childs play, but gradually escalates to a thick story with multiple endings, tough moral choices, emotional investment and interesting points for real life considerations.

It is fun, get it.
